title: How Creative Lawyers Are Rewriting the Rules With AI — Jen Leonard & Bridget McCormack on the Linklaters associate-builders (AAA, AI and the Future of Law)
pub: American Arbitration Association — AI and the Future of Law podcast
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source predicts that creative lawyers will become more prominent as AI develops, but it does not address dispute-resolution access, process redesign, machine adjudication versus human assistance, safeguards, legitimacy, or performance evidence. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.
qs: And today we’re going to talk about creative associates, which I’m really excited about because we predicted in our predictions episode that 2026 would be the year where creative lawyers really bring their talents to bear.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts that AI is likely to disrupt junior-level work and materially extends the cluster’s proposed response by advocating protected, resourced junior experimentation, client-problem-focused tool building and hybrid practice/technology careers. It does not directly develop the cluster’s verification-and-expertise paradox, so its contribution is chiefly an additional developmental model.
qs: I don’t see how it wouldn’t disrupt junior-level work.
You could do vibe lawyering with junior associates or summer associates, especially when they don’t yet have a billable hour requirement.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption depends on organisational absorption rather than tool access and materially extends this by advocating integrated lawyer-builder careers, cross-functional problem solving, leadership participation, protected experimentation time and real resources. Its supervised-agent forecasts are consistent with human oversight, while its reliance on Linklaters reporting remains appropriately tentative.
qs: It causes people to miss opportunities to see problems and solutions at the intersections, because everyone just sees what’s in their lane.
You also have to give people time and space to actually do it, not just say you want everyone doing it.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational absorption and materially develops that proposition by prescribing cross-functional participation, top-down and bottom-up engagement, protected experimentation time, resources and formal innovation structures. Its forecasts about junior-work disruption remain explicitly hypothetical and uncertain.
qs: You also have to give people time and space to actually do it, not just say you want everyone doing it.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI adoption is organisational change rather than a software purchase and materially develops the proposition with reported Linklaters examples of associate-led tools reaching firmwide use. It identifies culture, leadership, protected time, budgets and hybrid career paths as conditions for converting frontline experimentation into sustained institutional innovation, while treating effects on junior work and autonomous systems as unresolved.
qs: If you don’t create conditions where people feel psychologically safe and encouraged to experiment, then innovation only happens because of extraordinary people taking it on themselves.
You also have to give people time and space to actually do it, not just say you want everyone doing it.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Leonard and McCormack accept the cluster’s jagged-capability premise and materially develop its operating-model argument. Their hands-on experiments show uneven performance across tools, while their concrete prescription—top-down and bottom-up participation, protected time, resources and structured R&D—specifies how established firms can absorb AI rather than merely procure it. They do not substantially address verification, autonomy or labour-market effects.
qs: But I couldn’t figure out how to change the things I wanted to change—another jagged-edge problem.
You also have to give people time and space to actually do it, not just say you want everyone doing it.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the proposition that agentic legal value comes from applying AI to contextualised workflows rather than isolated text generation, while reinforcing the need for retained human accountability. Its eDiscovery example is hypothetical rather than measured, and it leaves supervision safeguards unresolved.
qs: I could imagine—maybe it’s already happening—if you’re a litigator in discovery on a small case, dropping all the documents into Claude, explaining what you’re looking for and the context of the engagement, and running eDiscovery far more efficiently.
Yes—and I’m not really sure what all of this agentic behavior means for the supervising lawyer, because the system is making decisions on its own.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s proposition that AI may automate traditional junior work, alter lawyers’ roles and broaden career paths while leaving supervision and implementation unresolved. Its claims are mainly forecasts and analogies rather than evidence of realised workforce or training outcomes.
qs: I don’t see how it wouldn’t disrupt junior-level work.
It makes me optimistic not just about improving practice, but about expanding career paths and letting lawyers exercise skills they haven’t always been able to use.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: Leonard and McCormack support the synthesis’s distinction between agentic output and autonomous legal practice. Leonard’s experiment produced substantial deliverables but still required human deployment, while they explicitly leave supervising-lawyer responsibilities unresolved. Their predictions about junior-work disruption and legal specialisation are analogical and prospective rather than evidence of autonomous legal deployment.
qs: I can’t activate the site myself, but I have all the HTML files.
Yes—and I’m not really sure what all of this agentic behavior means for the supervising lawyer, because the system is making decisions on its own.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Leonard and McCormack support the proposition that frontier-model providers are progressing from advice-generation toward direct execution of legal workflows. They anticipate Claude handling discovery and disrupting junior work, while treating these outcomes as analogical forecasts rather than measured legal results and flagging unresolved lawyer-supervision issues.
qs: It’s more agentic in the sense that Claude can take action on its own rather than just give advice.

I could imagine—maybe it’s already happening—if you’re a litigator in discovery on a small case, dropping all the documents into Claude, explaining what you’re looking for and the context of the engagement, and running eDiscovery far more efficiently.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source endorses practitioner-led experimentation and continued everyday testing rather than waiting for mature or certain technology. It links lawyer-built tools to improved practice and broader careers while treating agentic legal capabilities and acceleration as forecasts, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: That leads nicely into talking about creative lawyers—people who are identifying problems and experimenting with AI to build real tools.
So I thought, time to go back to the well.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the engagement-first proposition by anticipating that creative lawyers will actively apply their talents to AI. However, it offers only a prediction and preview, without examples, implementation guidance or evidence of outcomes, so it does not materially extend the cluster.
qs: And today we’re going to talk about creative associates, which I’m really excited about because we predicted in our predictions episode that 2026 would be the year where creative lawyers really bring their talents to bear.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports human-supervised augmentation that shifts lawyers away from routine work toward strategic judgment and meaningful tasks. Its vision is more agentic and prospective than the cluster’s bounded copilot framing, but it still retains human supervision and acknowledges human approval bottlenecks rather than advocating unsupervised substitution.
qs: If it can code autonomously, they can supervise the AI agents so humans can focus on higher-level strategic thinking—deciding what questions matter and what problems are worth solving.
There are a lot of things lawyers do that they’d be happy not to do, so they can focus on work that’s more meaningful and valuable.

kp.k: Frontier models show uneven, temperamental performance
kp.d: McCormack and Leonard describe materially different results from ChatGPT, Claude and Notebook LM on slide-deck creation. Their personal experiments suggest a continuing “jagged edge”: visual quality, substantive quality and editability do not consistently coincide, and Leonard expressly qualifies that she did not independently verify all AI-generated veterinary content.
qs: Notebook LM produced an unbelievably intricate, beautiful deck. The slides themselves were off the charts. The content was imperfect, and I’m sure there’s a way to fix that.

And Claude, by the way, did the best job for me. Substantively, it was really good. The slides were A-minus. But I couldn’t figure out how to change the things I wanted to change—another jagged-edge problem.
I don’t know whether all the content is accurate, but it was consistent with everything the vet told us, and I uploaded the discharge papers as another source.

kp.k: Claude Code enables more agentic software development
kp.d: Leonard characterizes Claude Code as an agentic system operating within a developer’s coding environment rather than merely responding to pasted snippets. She says it can inspect the broader code base, take actions with limited supervision and perform documentation, refactoring and boilerplate work, leaving developers to focus on higher-level strategy.
qs: Instead of having to do all of the copying and pasting that coders usually do back and forth with Claude to get it to work, this is a much more agentic system where Claude is working alongside them inside their actual coding environment.
It’s more agentic in the sense that Claude can take action on its own rather than just give advice.
It understands context extremely well because it can see the entire code base it’s working on, so its suggestions fit the whole project rather than just a snippet.
Claude Code also handles a lot of tedious but time-consuming work—updating documentation, refactoring code, setting up boilerplate—so developers can focus on higher-level strategy.

kp.k: Non-coders can build sophisticated digital products
kp.d: Leonard reports that, despite lacking coding skills, she used Claude Code for about three hours to redesign her company website. The system generated HTML files and developer documentation, although deployment and some formatting problems still required a human web developer; she also reports context degradation late in the session and upgrading from a $20 to a $100 monthly plan.
qs: I spent about three hours with Claude Code and couldn’t believe how beautiful it was.
It generated all the files I need to hand off to a web developer. I can’t activate the site myself, but I have all the HTML files.
It also generated a README for the developer with specs for fonts, colors, and two unresolved issues—our team photos were embedded in the HTML and not centered properly.
One thing people mention with Claude Code is that long conversations can degrade. That happened toward the end.
I upgraded to the $100-a-month plan from the $20 one—and honestly, it was unbelievable.

kp.k: Coding transformation provides an analogy for law
kp.d: The speakers use autonomous coding as analogy rather than direct legal-market evidence. Leonard compares AI’s removal of manual coding to the likely historical obsolescence of junior lawyers manually reviewing documents and creating privilege logs, while McCormack describes Claude Code as a major discontinuity for coding.
qs: This feels like the ChatGPT moment, but for coding.
People might look back and ask whether junior associates really used to sit in rooms with bankers boxes, manually reviewing documents, sorting them into piles, and creating privilege logs.
It sounds crazy now, but that’s what we used to do.

kp.k: Legal agents are predicted to automate junior work
kp.d: Leonard and McCormack predict, rather than demonstrate, that Claude Code-like legal agents will emerge. Leonard speculates that a litigator could give documents and engagement context to an agent to conduct small-case eDiscovery more efficiently, and says she does not see how this would avoid disrupting junior-level work. McCormack assumes frontier labs are already developing legal equivalents.
qs: I could imagine—maybe it’s already happening—if you’re a litigator in discovery on a small case, dropping all the documents into Claude, explaining what you’re looking for and the context of the engagement, and running eDiscovery far more efficiently.
I don’t see how it wouldn’t disrupt junior-level work.
So I assume Claude Code for legal is coming, and that they’re already working on it.
They’ve also said that coding isn’t where this ends; it’s where it starts.

kp.k: Agentic systems create supervision and contract questions
kp.d: Leonard flags unresolved professional and doctrinal issues arising when an AI agent makes decisions rather than only advising a lawyer. She specifically identifies uncertainty for the supervising lawyer and reports McCormack’s concern that autonomous agent decisions may complicate contract law’s traditional focus on a meeting of human minds; no legal resolution is offered.
qs: I’m not really sure what all of this agentic behavior means for the supervising lawyer, because the system is making decisions on its own.
You surfaced some additional questions about what it means for contract law itself—when an agent is making decisions, it’s no longer just a meeting of human minds.

kp.k: Human gating may constrain AI-driven acceleration
kp.d: The speakers argue that faster AI-supported discovery does not automatically accelerate implementation where human processes remain bottlenecks. Peer review and clinical trials are offered as examples, although Leonard speculates that AI might eventually accelerate some gating processes such as peer review itself.
qs: In academia, especially scientific research, there’s been a lot of discussion about how accelerating discovery doesn’t necessarily accelerate execution because of bottlenecks like peer review.
Those human gating moments slow everything down.
Even if you can’t speed up something like a clinical trial, are there ways to accelerate peer review itself?

kp.d: McCormack reports that Linklaters managing associate Tanya Sadoughi built a Python prototype to generate client-ready work-in-progress updates automatically from time records. According to the account, she developed it over one weekend in July, pitched it the following month, and it was used globally across the firm by the next year. The evidence is a podcast retelling of articles the hosts read, not an independent evaluation.
qs: So she built a tool that just generates those updates automatically from time records. You have a button, you press the button, and you get a client-ready summary.

She apparently worked on a Python prototype over one weekend in July, pitched it to her leadership the next month, and by the next year everybody across the firm was using her solution globally—like, everybody was using it.
According to her, she just taught herself how to code on weekends, in part because she believed she was going to need to upskill pretty aggressively.

kp.d: McCormack reports that Linklaters managing associate James Phoenix created an Excel plug-in using the firm’s internal chatbot, Leila, to flag and correct recurring errors in time-recording narratives before bills were issued. She says the tool was subsequently rolled out globally, presenting it as another associate-led response to tedious manual work.
qs: He was frustrated with mistakes they were seeing in their time-recording narratives, because that meant they had to do this really tedious manual review before they could actually send bills out—which makes sense.
So he built an Excel plug-in that uses their internal chatbot—apparently they call her Leila—to flag those issues and fix common narrative errors, things they see over and over again.
He vibe-coded a little Excel plug-in that uses another internal AI tool of theirs to do this, and that’s now rolled out globally across the firm.

kp.d: The speakers argue that natural-language or “vibe” coding allows lawyers without deep technical expertise to build tools by describing desired outcomes to AI. Leonard contrasts this with Sadoughi’s weekend Python learning and says the technical capability is already available to associates, while recognizing that adoption depends on organizational conditions.
qs: James used the term “vibe coding” when he was describing it. That’s the idea that you can just tell AI what you want and it will help you build it.
You don’t need deep technical skill—I don’t believe you do, and James said he doesn’t either.
The technical capability is already there. Any associate could be doing what James and Tanya did.
So I definitely think it lowers the bar—not having to do what Tanya did and teach yourself Python, but being able to dive right into it.

kp.k: Innovation requires safety, recognition and permission
kp.d: Leonard argues that most lawyers’ rule-following orientation and fear of departing from firm norms can suppress experimentation even when tools are accessible. She recommends a culture in which experimentation is celebrated, rewarded and psychologically safe, rather than relying on unusually entrepreneurial individuals to innovate without permission.
qs: They’re looking for problems, and they’re not waiting for permission to solve them.
Most lawyers, to overgeneralize, are not temperamentally suited to that. They tend to be rules-followers.
So I think creating a culture where this kind of experimentation is celebrated and rewarded is step one.
If you don’t create conditions where people feel psychologically safe and encouraged to experiment, then innovation only happens because of extraordinary people taking it on themselves.

kp.d: Leonard uses an anecdote about a 1990s litigator being told not to use Control-F to illustrate how faster methods may threaten established firm practices and the billable-hour model. The example supports her broader claim that technical capacity alone will not produce adoption when organizational incentives resist efficiency.
qs: I remember a mutual friend of ours talking about how, when he was a litigator in the ’90s, he used Control-F and told the partner, “We could do this so much faster.”
And the partner was like, “Don’t do that. This is how we do it,” because it impacts the billing model and feels threatening.

kp.k: Hybrid legal and innovation careers should remain possible
kp.d: The speakers oppose forcing lawyers to choose among substantive practice, technology and operations. Leonard reports that Linklaters supplied the associate-builders with teams, budgets and innovation-team secondments, while allowing Sadoughi to combine technology projects with practice. McCormack argues that rigid lanes obscure problems and solutions found at professional intersections.
qs: Linklaters in this case—based on the articles we read—gave both associates resources. They gave them teams and budgets.
I thought it was really interesting that in both cases these associates were seconded to their innovation teams.
I really agree with lawyers who don’t like having to choose a path, and I think that’s still fairly common—choosing between the AI or tech side, operations, or substantive legal work.
It causes people to miss opportunities to see problems and solutions at the intersections, because everyone just sees what’s in their lane.

kp.k: Firm innovation must be structured and resourced
kp.d: McCormack recommends both top-down and bottom-up participation: leaders should visibly experiment with AI, while firms must provide protected time, space and resources. She identifies partnership R&D as difficult and argues that stated encouragement without changed expectations or actual support is insufficient.
qs: I’ve said this a million times—it has to be top-down and bottom-up.
Whoever the managing partner is needs to be vibe-coding herself, showing where she’s succeeding and where she’s not, and getting people excited about it.
You also have to give people time and space to actually do it, not just say you want everyone doing it.
R&D is hard for partnerships, and that requires thought. Innovation happens when it’s structured.

kp.k: Legal education should teach problem-led experimentation
kp.d: Leonard proposes a “vibe lawyering” course in which students identify professional problems, build AI-assisted responses and share lessons. The speakers extend the recommendation to liberal-arts students, court-based access-to-justice problems, junior associates and summer programs using accumulated client-feedback data, particularly where participants do not yet face billable-hour requirements.
qs: I could imagine a vibe lawyering class, where you bring in students and either share major problems from the profession and have them tackle them, or they come with their own problems, find a problem, vibe-lawyer around it, and share what they learn.
Send them to the debt-collection docket at the local court and then send them off to vibe-lawyer for four days and see what they come up with.
All of these firms do extensive feedback surveys with their clients. They have years of data on client pain points.
You could do vibe lawyering with junior associates or summer associates, especially when they don’t yet have a billable hour requirement.

kp.k: AI may expand lawyers’ roles and career paths
kp.d: Leonard presents AI-enabled building as a way for lawyers to exercise previously underused creative and entrepreneurial skills, improve practice and broaden career options. McCormack frames the examples optimistically as evidence that lawyers can shed unwanted tasks and concentrate on more meaningful, valuable and strategic work, although these are forward-looking judgments rather than measured outcomes.
qs: It makes me optimistic not just about improving practice, but about expanding career paths and letting lawyers exercise skills they haven’t always been able to use.
There are a lot of things lawyers do that they’d be happy not to do, so they can focus on work that’s more meaningful and valuable.
I think we could never have done this in our junior lawyer days because the tech just wasn’t there.
No, this really is the best timeline—even for lawyers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard predicts that agentic AI will make discovery more efficient and disrupt junior-level legal work; McCormack expects legal-specific agentic tools to follow coding tools.
pts.d: Leonard imagines a litigator supplying documents and engagement context to an agent for discovery in a small case. She presents junior-work disruption as an expected consequence, not a measured employment outcome. McCormack assumes that a legal counterpart to Claude Code is already being developed and will allow lawyers to concentrate on more meaningful, valuable work. The exchange raises a possible six-month horizon as a question, but does not establish a firm release prediction. Leonard explicitly leaves unresolved what autonomous system decisions mean for lawyer supervision and contract law.

pts.k: McCormack reports that a Linklaters associate automated work-in-progress and fee updates, replacing a tedious manual production process.
pts.d: McCormack describes Tanya Sadoughi, a London banking and finance managing associate, building a tool that generates client-ready summaries from time records. The claimed benefit is faster production of information clients and partners already want, rather than a change to substantive legal advice. McCormack reports that a weekend Python prototype progressed to global firm use. This is a secondhand implementation account, not a quantified productivity study.

pts.k: McCormack reports that an associate-built AI plug-in flags and corrects recurring time-recording narrative errors before billing.
pts.d: McCormack describes litigation and investigations managing associate James Phoenix using vibe coding to build an Excel plug-in connected to Linklaters’ internal chatbot, Leila. The tool addresses errors previously requiring tedious manual review before bills could be sent. She reports global rollout, but supplies no measured reduction in review time, error rates or billing costs, and does not say that all human review was eliminated.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack argue that AI-assisted coding lowers the technical barrier to lawyer-led innovation.
pts.d: McCormack explains vibe coding as describing a desired tool to AI rather than requiring deep technical skill. Leonard agrees that this broadens participation beyond lawyers who independently learn Python and claims that the technical capability is already available to associates. Leonard also recalls their prediction that 2026 would be the year creative lawyers bring their talents to bear. These are capability and participation claims supported by examples and experience, not evidence that every associate can independently deploy production-ready software.

pts.k: The speakers argue that broad-based legal innovation depends on institutional incentives, resources and psychological safety, not technical availability alone.
pts.d: Leonard says experimentation must be celebrated and rewarded because many lawyers are rule-followers who may find departures from firm norms threatening. She links resistance to an anecdote about a partner rejecting a faster search method because it affected billing. McCormack calls for leadership participation, protected time and resources, noting that partnership R&D is difficult. Leonard reports that Linklaters provided teams, budgets and innovation secondments. Both argue against forcing lawyers to choose between practice and technology: combining them can expand careers and reveal problems and solutions across organisational boundaries.

pts.k: Leonard proposes AI-enabled problem-solving classes and associate programmes as ways to address legal-service and client pain points.
pts.d: Leonard imagines a 'vibe lawyering' class in which students build around professional problems and share their learning. She also proposes giving junior or summer associates problems drawn from client feedback, particularly before billable-hour requirements apply. McCormack extends the proposal to non-law students observing a debt-collection docket and then experimenting for four days. These are prospective educational and service-design suggestions, not reports of implemented programmes or demonstrated access-to-justice gains.

pts.k: McCormack suggests that an AI arbitrator could participate in dispute boards and that the dispute-board model could extend beyond construction.
pts.d: McCormack presents AI participation as something she wants to explore, not as an established deployment. She reasons from the reported success of early dispute intervention in large construction projects and suggests life sciences as another possible setting. Her claim about AI's contribution remains an exploratory hypothesis; the transcript supplies no operational example, performance evidence or adoption timetable.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on secondhand deployment stories, firsthand tool use and analogy, rather than quantitative legal-performance or labour-market evidence.
pts.d: The Linklaters accounts come from articles the speakers read; the associates are not interviewed in this transcript. Leonard’s firsthand experience building website files with Claude Code supports her view that non-coders can create useful artefacts, but she still required a developer to activate the site and resolve issues. Her experience is not a legal-work benchmark. Predictions about legal agents extrapolate from coding tools, health-model development and unspecified researcher comments. McCormack’s slide-deck experiments also reveal uneven content, formatting and editability. No measured legal time savings, costs, accuracy rates, employment changes or client outcomes are supplied. External quotations are contextual support, not treated here as independently established claims by those quoted.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source combines reported current deployments, a broad 2026 prediction and undated expectations about legal agents, with substantial implementation conditions.
pts.d: In this 2026 episode, both Linklaters tools are described as already rolled out globally. Sadoughi’s sequence is a July weekend prototype, leadership pitch the following month and global use by the next year; exact calendar years are not provided. The speakers’ creative-lawyer prediction explicitly concerns 2026. A legal counterpart to Claude Code is anticipated without a definite date; six months appears in McCormack’s question rather than a settled forecast. Wider uptake is conditional on protected time, budgets, leadership example and permission to experiment. Leonard’s website trial required a subscription upgrade and developer handoff, and she reports deterioration in a long conversation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are associates, supervising lawyers, law-firm clients and partners, innovation teams, and legal educators.
pts.d: Junior lawyers face disruption to routine discovery work while gaining opportunities to build tools and pursue hybrid practice-and-technology careers. Managing associates are the reported innovators in the Linklaters examples. Partners and clients receive automated progress and fee summaries; billing staff and lawyers gain assistance with narrative corrections. Firm leaders must support experimentation and allocate resources despite partnership and billing incentives. Law schools and summer programmes are proposed sites for developing problem-solving skills. Parties to major projects are prospective beneficiaries of AI-assisted dispute boards. Debt-collection court users appear as a possible focus for student experimentation, not as demonstrated beneficiaries. The source gives no quantified headcount, staffing-leverage or legal-market-share forecast.
